n: Fourteen years later Paul returned to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, a Gentile convert. Many link this with the Jerusalem council in Acts 15.
He went by revelation and privately laid out his gospel before the leading apostles, to be sure his work among Gentiles was in harmony with theirs.

f.g: The recognized leaders of the Church.

n: Yet the leaders didn’t require Titus, a Greek, to be circumcised — a test case proving Gentiles needn’t live the law of Moses.
The issue arose because false believers had slipped in to spy on the freedom believers have in Christ, hoping to enslave them under the law.
Paul didn’t yield to them for a moment, so the true gospel would be preserved for the Galatians.
The respected leaders — whatever their standing, which God doesn’t weigh — added nothing to Paul’s message.
Instead they recognized that Paul had been entrusted with the gospel to the Gentiles, as Peter had been to the Jews.
The same God who worked through Peter among Jews worked powerfully through Paul among Gentiles.
James, Peter, and John, the pillars of the Church, recognized God’s grace in Paul and shook hands with him and Barnabas in fellowship, dividing their missionary focus.

f.g: Main supports — key leaders of the Church.
A handshake signaling formal agreement and partnership.

n: Their only request was that Paul remember the poor — something he was eager to do.
Later, when Peter came to Antioch, Paul confronted him to his face because Peter was clearly in the wrong.

f.g: Antioch in Syria, an early center of Gentile Christianity.

n: Peter had been eating with Gentile believers, but when men came from James, he pulled back, afraid of the circumcision party.

f.w: he did eat with the Gentiles
them which were of the circumcision
f.g: Jewish Christians who insisted on the law of Moses.

n: Other Jewish believers joined in this hypocrisy, and even Barnabas was swept along.
Paul publicly asked Peter: if you, a Jew, live like a Gentile, how can you force Gentiles to live like Jews? Even an apostle could be corrected about how a principle was applied.

f.g: Weren’t walking straight in line with the gospel.

n: Paul continues: we were born Jews, not Gentile “sinners” as Jews then labeled outsiders.

f.g: A common Jewish label for those outside the covenant law.

n: Yet even Jews know a person is put right with God not by keeping the law’s works but through faith in Jesus Christ. No one is justified by the law.

f.w: not justified by the works of the law

f.g: Declared righteous; brought into right relationship with God.

n: If seeking justification in Christ shows we are sinners (by the law’s standard), does that make Christ promote sin? Absolutely not!

f.g: A servant or promoter of sin.

n: If Paul rebuilt the system of law he had torn down, he would prove himself a lawbreaker.

f.w: build again the things which I destroyed
f.g: Restore the law as a way to be justified.

n: Through the law he died to the law, so he could live for God. The law itself pointed him to Christ.
Paul’s old self was crucified with Christ. Now Christ lives in him, and his mortal life is lived by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave Himself for him.

f.w: who loved me, and gave himself for me

n: Paul won’t set aside God’s grace. If righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing.
